title: What is an allergen?
plain_explanation: An allergen is usually a protein that some people’s immune system mistakes as harmful. In an allergic person, the immune system makes IgE antibodies that recognise that protein. The food itself is not always the problem—the specific protein inside it can be.

title: How does an allergic reaction happen?
plain_explanation: First, the immune system becomes sensitised: it makes IgE antibodies against a protein. On a later exposure, the protein binds those IgE antibodies on mast cells. The mast cells then release chemicals such as histamine, which can cause itching, swelling, hives, gut symptoms, or breathing problems.

title: Why can birch pollen make apple cause itching?
plain_explanation: Some proteins in birch pollen look similar to proteins in raw fruits such as apple. If your immune system has learned to react to birch pollen, it may sometimes react to the similar apple protein too. This is called cross-reactivity.

title: Does cooking always make a food safe?
plain_explanation: No. Heating changes some allergen proteins, especially PR-10 proteins, so some people tolerate cooked fruit better. But other allergens, such as many lipid-transfer proteins, 2S albumins, caseins and tropomyosins, can be more heat-stable. Only a clinician can help assess what is safe for you.

title: Not every reaction is cross-reactivity
plain_explanation: A bad reaction to a food does not always mean cross-reactivity, and it does not always mean allergy. It could be food intolerance, a stomach or gut condition, an infection, irritation, contamination, or another medical issue. This website explains possible protein-based reasons for symptoms; it does not diagnose allergy.

title: This website is educational only
plain_explanation: This website is an educational explainer. It cannot diagnose an allergy, predict how severe a reaction will be, or tell you whether a food is safe. For personal advice, testing, or an emergency plan, speak with a doctor or allergy specialist.
